playbook:
I treat it as a stock-building problem until the final round, then as a liquidation problem.

- When 2+ seasons remain, I set catch = the displayed sustainable share, rounded to one decimal. No tilt, no "making up ground."
- When the other two boats repeatedly land above the share, I still anchor on the share and add only a small premium (at most ~10–15%). I don't chase; the high stock is the asset. In this run one rival escalated (12.0 → 12.5 → 14.0) while the other drifted down toward the share — the cadence still held the stock at ~84 entering the final season, well above the risk zone.
- When total landed = share for everyone, I keep the cadence and let regrowth do the scoring. I resist grabbing early — a +3 grab in a mid season costs roughly the same in lost regrowth and signals escalation.
- When the stock gets meaningfully below ~60 before the end, I tighten to slightly under the share so the last-round stock stays worth harvesting.
- Entering the final season, I switch objective to clearing the pool: estimate the rivals' likely final bids from their trends (in this run ~10 and ~14, escalating) and bid (remaining stock − their expected bids − a small buffer). With 83.6 on the table that argued for ~29, which is what I bid; no reason to leave more than their expected take behind. If rivals have been consistently greedy, shave the buffer; if passive, take a bit less than the max to avoid a zero-stock wipeout risk from rounding.
- Don't overthink mid-season messages: one-line arithmetic, end on the bracket token. No confessions, no extra market talk. A bare token reply is fine when nothing has changed.

1.text:
When the game opens with a regenerating shared resource, I commit to harvesting at or just above the sustainable share — the regrowth math makes conservation the dominant strategy for total score, not a moral choice. A small premium (1–2 fish over the share) from season 1 is safe and free value when the stock is at or near cap.

Before each submission I do the quick arithmetic: current stock, post-harvest regrowth, seasons remaining. I never take an amount that, combined with plausible rival takes, would push the stock toward zero — collapse is the only outcome that ruins me regardless of my relative position.

When I'm behind on total score, I increase my take modestly (roughly 1.2–1.5x the sustainable share), not aggressively. I size my aggression to what the stock can survive even if others grab too.

When I'm ahead, I defend by fishing exactly at the sustainable share or slightly below — there's no reason to risk collapse to widen a lead, and restraint pulls rivals toward restraint too.

I watch the landed history for each rival's pattern. Rivals stable at the sustainable share tell me the stock will hold, so I can safely take a small premium every mid-game season. If a rival spikes hard, I don't match — I wait for them to settle before pressing my own premium.

Through the middle seasons I bank a consistent small premium (share plus 2–4) rather than alternating restraint and spikes — against cooperative rivals this accumulates a lead without ever testing the stock.

I go heavy only when the endgame makes regrowth irrelevant: in the final season there is no future to protect, so I take a large share of what's left. What still needs sharpening: my final grab of 27 from an 83.6 stock left roughly a third of the stock unharvested by me. In a clear final season with a known history of moderate rivals, I should estimate their likely takes from recent seasons and take close to (stock − expected rival takes), not a conservative round number. Even a take of 40+ would have been safe against rivals landing ~10.

I keep any reasoning in my reply short and always end with the required bracketed token.

2.text:
- When a season opens, I first compute the safe default: stock divided by boats, roughly the stated sustainable share. That is my anchor every season, not my opening bid.
- In the first season, when no one has revealed a style yet, I do NOT spike. I take exactly the sustainable share — not even a notch above. My +0.9 premium in season 1 bought almost nothing and contributed to a stock decline that ran all game. Bank information, not fish.
- When other boats take the sustainable share, I take the sustainable share. Matched restraint keeps the regrowth base large, and the flowing payoff exceeds any one-season grab.
- I track the total take, not just my own. The break-even is when total catch equals the regrowth the stock would produce. If one boat consistently takes above share (boat 3 took 12 then 14 while the share fell to 9.3), the commons erodes even while each individual looks "reasonable" — our stock slid 100 → 83.6 on nothing but small overshoots.
- When the stock falls two seasons running, I cut toward or below my share even if rivals overfish — but cutting alone didn't work this game: the decline continued because I only trimmed ~5%. Next time, if one rival is the clear overshoot and the stock keeps falling, I cut meaningfully below my share once (10–20%) as a visible signal, then hold at share. A survivor in a live fishery beats a leader in a dead one.
- Rivals with a cooperative track record may still defect late. Boat 3 held ~share for four seasons, then took 14 in season 5. From season N-1 onward I assume someone will grab, and I make my terminal plan one season early instead of being surprised.
- I never take a large grab unless it is the final season or the stock is heading to zero regardless of what I do. Spikes signal aggression and invite retaliation.
- In the final season, with no future to protect: if the stock is ample I take a disciplined terminal haul up to about a third of the stock minus a safety margin — not the naive maximum, and certainly not the sustainable share. My 25 from 83.6 was right; leaving 58.6 to regrow nobody would ever harvest would have been a waste by ~15+ points.
- I size any non-final premium small (at most ~15–25% above share, and only while total take stays below break-even and the stock is stable or rising). If those conditions fail, I revert to at-or-below share immediately.
- What did not work: tiny premiums stacked on other boats' tiny premiums. Individually defensible, collectively they drained the commons every season. My edge must come from an accurate read of aggregate take plus a well-timed terminal haul, not from being permanently the "+1" boat.
- Each decision, I ask in order: Is this season N or N-1? Then shift toward terminal harvesting, sized to the stock. If not, is total take at or below break-even? Then hold at share. If not, cut first.
